title: Forgets to eat
hook: Confucius describes himself as someone so eager to learn he forgets his food (Analects 7.18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Qing the woodworker, who fasted until reward and praise fell away. Your line was forget the prize. Today, another kind of forgetting, from another Chinese teacher. Day nine hundred two.

Somebody asks your friend what you're really like, and your friend says nothing. Just stands there. Later, you hear about it. That's the scene in the Analects, the book of Confucius's sayings. A nobleman, the Duke of She, asks one of Confucius's students, Zilu, what kind of man his teacher is. Zilu doesn't answer. When Confucius finds out, he doesn't scold. He tells Zilu what he could have said. And the self-portrait he offers isn't of a sage or a statesman. It's a portrait Confucius offers of himself. Today's word is the student who stayed silent: Zilu.
screen: `WHAT'S HE REALLY LIKE?` → `ZILU SAYS NOTHING.` → `A MAN WHO FORGETS TO EAT.`

segments.voice: First, the description, in paraphrase. Why didn't you tell him, Confucius says, that I'm simply a man who, in his eagerness to learn, forgets his food; who, in the joy of it, forgets his worries; and who doesn't notice old age coming on? Three forgettings. Food. Sorrow. Age. Second, what's being chased. The line itself just says eagerness, but Legge and the commentators read it as eagerness to learn. Not power, not money. Learning, the steady work of study and practice that runs through the Analects. For Confucius, that work wasn't a chore to get through. In this passage, it's what he loses himself in. Third, notice the joy. He doesn't say he forgets food because he's grimly disciplined. He says the joy of it makes him forget his troubles. The eagerness comes first, and the forgetting follows. Nobody has to hide his tools or take away his plate. The hours just go. Fourth, how this sits next to yesterday. Qing the woodworker had to fast for days to forget reward and praise. Confucius describes something that arrives on its own when the work itself is loved. Two different roads to the same quiet place, where the clock and the stomach go silent for a while. And it's worth saying the honest part: the Analects doesn't recommend skipping meals. Elsewhere it records Confucius as careful about his food. This is a portrait of absorption, not a rule about lunch. A version of it can turn up anywhere. A puzzle, a garden, a song, a page of notes, and suddenly the window has gone dark.
screen: `FOOD, SORROW, AGE: FORGOTTEN.` · `WHAT HE CHASES IS LEARNING.` · `JOY COMES FIRST.` · `ABSORPTION, NOT A RULE.` · then, large: `FORGETS TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle into its own rhythm. Think back to a time you lost track of the hours doing something. Maybe recently, maybe long ago. What were you doing? Where were you sitting? What did your hands do? Let that memory fill in. Then ask: is there something like that within reach today, even for twenty minutes? Choose it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Zilu. The student who didn't answer when asked what kind of man Confucius was, and what Confucius told him he could have said. Today's word.
Your line: forget the hours. Today, lose yourself in one task, long enough that you look up surprised at the time. Day nine hundred two.

screen: `DAY 902 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT IT COSTS IN LIFE.`

howItsDone: Readers of the Analects, in Confucian schools and families and in classrooms, turn to this passage as Confucius's own picture of a life given to learning.

fork.setup: you're Zilu. a duke asks you what your teacher is really like. Confucius later tells you what you could have said. what was it?
options: he's the wisest man in the land.
he's a man so eager to learn he forgets to eat.
he's a great official who should be given office.
fork.reveal: his self-portrait: a man who forgets his food in eagerness, forgets his worries in joy, and doesn't notice old age coming.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man so busy he skips lunch.
what it means: Confucius's self-portrait, so absorbed in learning that food, worry and age slip out of mind.
what a scholar hears: Analects 7.18 in Legge's numbering, a passage where Confucius describes himself, prompted by a student's silence before the Duke of She.

notes: Analects 7.18 paraphrased rather than quoting Legge, to avoid misquoting. Numbering differs between editions (7.18 Legge / 7.19 others).
'Elsewhere it records Confucius as careful about his food' refers to Analects book 10 (e.g. 10.8); confirm reference.
Trapdoor calls it 'a passage where Confucius describes himself': softened from 'a rare passage'.
Teach ends on absorption examples rather than any claim about how many people experience it.
Editor: cut the uncited claim that the Analects was gathered by his followers.

Audit: 7.18 does not name the object of Confucius's eagerness (fa fen); Legge supplies '(of knowledge)' in brackets. The teach now says the line says eagerness and that Legge and commentators read it as learning, instead of presenting 'learning' as the text's own word. Keeper: confirm 'the commentators' phrasing.
